question: As per the Union Budget 2025-26, what is the target for nuclear power capacity of India by 2047?
solution:
The correct answer is __**100GW**__.

 [IMAGE: https://cdn.repeatermock.com/tb/36f36cd5ece4186095afcf2ffbfb7b80cc04b6c2e3226e7477a419a9fbc96f85.png] **__Key Points__**

__
 
• **Union Budget 2025-26** outlines India’s ambitious target of achieving **100 GW nuclear power capacity** by the year **2047**, marking the centenary of Indian independence.
 
• The target aligns with India’s commitment to transitioning towards **clean energy**, reducing dependence on fossil fuels, and meeting the **net-zero emission goals** by **2070**.
 
• **Nuclear energy** is prioritized due to its ability to provide **reliable, base-load power** with minimal carbon emissions, contributing to India’s sustainability agenda.
 
• India currently has a nuclear power capacity of approximately **7.48 GW** across **22 reactors**, and the expansion plan includes setting up new reactors and utilizing advanced technologies like **Fast Breeder Reactors (FBRs)** and **Small Modular Reactors (SMRs)**.
 
• The government is actively promoting **indigenous development** of nuclear technology under the **“Make in India” initiative** to reduce dependency on foreign expertise and create domestic employment opportunities.

 [IMAGE: https://cdn.repeatermock.com/tb/f13e2ad6582c16aa62a83672e2547ad20a01fddb61962a1acce42eb9a1a99caa.png] **Additional Information__**

__
 
• **Current Status of Nuclear Power in India:**

 
 
• India has **22 operational nuclear reactors**, primarily located in states like **Tamil Nadu**, **Maharashtra**, **Rajasthan**, and **Gujarat**.
 
• The largest nuclear power plant in India is the **Kudankulam Nuclear Power Plant**, located in Tamil Nadu, which is being expanded with Russian collaboration.
 
• India ranks **14th globally** in terms of installed nuclear power capacity.
 
 
 
• **Advantages of Nuclear Power:**
 
 
• **Low greenhouse gas emissions:** Nuclear energy generates electricity with minimal carbon footprint compared to fossil fuels.
 
• **High energy density:** A small amount of nuclear fuel can produce a vast amount of energy.
 
• **Reliable base-load power:** Unlike renewable sources like solar and wind, nuclear power plants provide consistent electricity output.
 
• **Long-term sustainability:** Advanced reactor technologies like FBRs utilize uranium more efficiently, reducing waste.
 
 
 
• **Challenges in Nuclear Power Expansion:**
 
 
• **High initial capital cost:** Building nuclear power plants requires significant investment in infrastructure and technology.
 
• **Safety concerns:** Nuclear accidents like Chernobyl and Fukushima have raised global concerns about reactor safety.
 
• **Radioactive waste management:** The disposal and long-term storage of nuclear waste remain a critical issue.
 
• **Public opposition:** Resistance from local communities due to environmental and safety concerns can delay projects.
 
 
 
• **Key Government Initiatives:**
 
 
• The ** is the central public sector enterprise responsible for the development and operation of nuclear power plants.
 
• Under the ,” India collaborates with countries like Russia, France, and the USA** for reactor technology and fuel supply.
 
• The **” regulates nuclear energy in India, ensuring safe and peaceful usage.
 
• India is a member of the , which oversees nuclear safety and security worldwide.
 
 
 
• Global Perspective:**
 
 
• Countries like **France** and **USA** heavily rely on nuclear energy, with France generating over **70% of its electricity** from nuclear power.
 
• China is rapidly expanding its nuclear capacity, targeting **70 GW** by **2035**.
 
• The **European Union** has included nuclear energy under its **“Green Taxonomy**” for sustainable investment.
 
 

 [IMAGE: https://cdn.repeatermock.com/tb/4f750a2730aad0987b5e719f277ddc90129c657928205c4d3b5aa23049023fa5.png] **Important Points__**

 
• **Fast Breeder Reactors (FBRs):**

 
 
• India’s **Prototype Fast Breeder Reactor (PFBR)** in Kalpakkam is expected to play a vital role in achieving the nuclear capacity target.
 
• FBRs offer higher fuel efficiency by utilizing **plutonium** and **uranium-238** from spent fuel.
 
 
 
• **Small Modular Reactors (SMRs):**
 
 
• SMRs are compact reactors with **lower construction costs** and **shorter installation times**, making them suitable for remote areas.
 
• India is exploring SMR technology for decentralized power generation.
 
 
 
• **Thorium Utilization:**
 
 
• India possesses **25% of the world’s thorium reserves**, and research is underway to use thorium in advanced reactors.
 
• Thorium-based reactors are safer and produce less nuclear waste compared to uranium-based reactors.
 
 
 
• **Role of Renewable Energy:**
 
 
• While nuclear power is significant, India also focuses on expanding its **solar, wind, and hydroelectric power** capacity to achieve energy security.
 
• The **” targets 280 GW** of solar power by **2030**.
